studies.title: Combined L-carnosine and L-tyrosine supplementation as an ergogenic strategy for physical and cognitive performance under fatigue in professional football playe
studies.abstract:
Background/objectives

Football performance depends on the integration of high-intensity neuromuscular output with rapid decision-making and executive control. Although L-carnosine (L-CAR) and L-tyrosine (L-TYR) have independently demonstrated ergogenic and neurocognitive benefits, evidence regarding their combined effects on both physical and cognitive performance under post-exercise fatigue in football-specific contexts remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the acute effects of L-CAR, L-TYR, and their combined supplementation on physical and cognitive performance following high-intensity exercise in professional football players.

Methods

Twenty-four male professionals completed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial involving four conditions (L-CAR, L-TYR, L-CAR+L-TYR, placebo). After supplementation, participants completed a Wingate-based fatigue protocol to assess anaerobic performance (peak power, mean power), followed by sprint tests (10-30 m; sprint time), an agility assessment (completion time), and football-specific passing accuracy tasks (execution time and accuracy). Executive function was evaluated using the Stroop test, including reaction time and error rates under neutral, congruent, and incongruent conditions.

Results

L-CAR significantly enhanced anaerobic power and agility, whereas L-TYR primarily improved cognitive performance. The combined condition produced the most pronounced effects, increasing peak power by ~17% and average power by ~16% versus placebo, reducing sprint and agility times by ~7-13%, and shortening incongruent Stroop reaction time by ~15%. Perceived exertion was lower with combined supplementation, while blood lactate concentrations did not differ significantly between conditions.

studies.title: Impact of L-theanine and L-tyrosine on markers of stress and cognitive performance in response to a virtual reality based active shooter training drill.
studies.abstract: Ingestion of L-theanine and L-tyrosine has been shown to reduce salivary stress biomarkers and improve aspects of cognitive performance in response to stress. However, there have been no studies to concurrently examine the impact of both L-theanine and L-tyrosine ingestion during a mental stress challenge (MSC) involving a brief cognitive challenge and a virtual reality based active shooter training drill. Thus, the purpose of this study was to determine the impact of ingestion of L-theanine and L-tyrosine on markers of stress and cognitive performance in response to a virtual reality active shooter drill and cognitive challenge. The cognitive challenge involved a Stroop challenge and mental arithmetic. Eighty subjects (age = 21 ± 2.6 yrs; male = 46; female = 34) were randomly assigned L-tyrosine (n = 28; 2000 mg), L-theanine (n = 25; 200 mg), or placebo (n = 27) prior to MSC exposure. Saliva samples, state-anxiety inventory (SAI) scales, and heart rate (HR) were collected before and after exposure to the MSC. Saliva was analyzed for stress markers α-amylase (sAA) and secretory immunoglobulin A (SIgA). The MSC resulted in significant increases in sAA, SIgA, HR, and SAI. Ingestion of L-theanine and L-tyrosine did not impact markers of stress. However, the L-tyrosine treatment demonstrated significantly lower missed responses compared to the placebo treatment group during the Stroop challenge. These data demonstrate that ingestion of L-theanine or L-tyrosine does not impact markers of stress in response to a MSC but may impact cognitive performance. This study was pre-registered as a clinical trial ("Impact of supplements on stress markers": NCT05592561).

studies.title: Baseline-dependent effect of dopamine's precursor L-tyrosine on working memory gating but not updating.
studies.abstract: Adaptive goal-directed behavior requires a dynamic balance between maintenance and updating within working memory (WM). This balance is controlled by an input-gating mechanism implemented by dopamine in the basal ganglia. Given that dopaminergic manipulations can modulate performance on WM-related tasks, it is important to gain mechanistic insight into whether such manipulations differentially affect updating (i.e., encoding and removal) and the closely-related gate opening/closing processes that respectively enable/prevent updating. To clarify this issue, 2.0 g of dopamine's precursor L-tyrosine was administered to healthy young adults (N = 45) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subjects study. WM processes were empirically distinguished using the reference-back paradigm, which isolates performance related to updating, gate opening, and gate closing. L-tyrosine had a selective, baseline-dependent effect only on gate opening, which was evidenced by markedly reduced variance across subjects in gate opening performance in the L-tyrosine compared with the placebo condition, whereas the whole-sample average performance did not differ between conditions. This indicates a pattern of results whereby low-performing subjects improved, whereas high-performing subjects were impaired on L-tyrosine. Importantly, this inverted U-shaped pattern was not explained by regression to the mean. These results are consistent with an inverted-U relationship between dopamine and WM, and they indicate that updating and gating are differentially affected by a dopaminergic manipulation. This highlights the importance of distinguishing these processes when studying WM, for example, in the context of WM deficits in disorders with a dopaminergic pathophysiology.

studies.title: A Double Blind, Randomized Cross-Over Trial of Tyrosine Treatment on Cognitive Function and Psychological Parameters in Severe Hospitalized Anorexia Nervosa Pat
studies.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by self-induced malnutrition, affecting body image, mood, cognition and survival. Tyrosine, an essential amino acid is the precursor of catecholamines. The use of tyrosine to treat AN is based on experiments on diet restricted mice, in which it increased food consumption, improved cognitive function and elevated brain catecholamines. We evaluated the effect of oral tyrosine administration on the cognition and emotional state of patients with AN. We hypothesized that tyrosine may improve cognitive function without changing body weight, thus "kick-start" nutritional rehabilitation. 19 female hospitalized patients with chronic AN were supplemented with L-tyrosine (100 mg/kg/day)/ placebo capsules for a three-week period in a double blind, randomized, cross-over study. Participants were evaluated cognitively and psychologically. Tyrosine shortened reaction time and test duration in memory tasks and improved depressive mood. No side effects were noted with the use of tyrosine. Tyrosine may improve cognitive function and psychological traits associated with AN.

studies.title: Food for thought: association between dietary tyrosine and cognitive performance in younger and older adults.
studies.abstract: The fact that tyrosine increases dopamine availability that, in turn, may enhance cognitive performance has led to numerous studies on healthy young participants taking tyrosine as a food supplement. As a result of this dietary intervention, participants show performance increases in working memory and executive functions. However, the potential association between habitual dietary tyrosine intake and cognitive performance has not been investigated to date. The present study aims at clarifying the association of episodic memory (EM), working memory (WM) and fluid intelligence (Gf), and tyrosine intake in younger and older adults. To this end, we acquired habitual tyrosine intake (food frequency questionnaire) from 1724 participants of the Berlin Aging Study II (1383 older adults, 341 younger adults) and modelled its relations to cognitive performance assessed in a broad battery of cognitive tasks using structural equation modeling. We observed a significant association between tyrosine intake and the latent factor capturing WM, Gf, and EM in the younger and the older sample. Due to partial strong factorial invariance between age groups for a confirmatory factor analysis on cognitive performance, we were able to compare the relationship between tyrosine and cognition between age groups and found no difference. Above and beyond previous studies on tyrosine food supplementation the present result extend this to a cross-sectional association between habitual tyrosine intake levels in daily nutrition and cognitive performance (WM, Gf, and EM). This corroborates nutritional recommendations that are thus far derived from single-dose administration studies.

studies.title: Failure of oral tyrosine supplementation to improve exercise performance in the heat.
studies.abstract: Acute oral tyrosine administration has been associated with increased constant-load, submaximal exercise capacity in the heat. This study sought to determine whether self-paced exercise performance in the heat is enhanced with the same tyrosine dosage. After familiarization, seven male endurance-trained volunteers, unacclimated to exercise in the heat, performed two experimental trials in 30°C (60% relative humidity) in a crossover fashion separated by at least 7 d. Subjects ingested 150 mg·kg(-1) body mass tyrosine (TYR) or an isocaloric quantity of whey powder (PLA) in 500 mL of sugar-free flavored water in a randomized, double-blind fashion. Sixty minutes after drink ingestion, the subjects cycled for 60 min at 57% ± 4% peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) and then performed a simulated cycling time trial requiring completion of an individualized target work quantity (393.1 ± 39.8 kJ). The ratio of plasma tyrosine plus phenylalanine (tyrosine precursor) to amino acids competing for brain uptake (free-tryptophan, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, threonine, and lysine) increased 2.5-fold from rest in TYR and remained elevated throughout exercise (P < 0.001), whereas it declined in PLA from rest to preexercise (P = 0.004). Time-trial power output (P = 0.869) and performance (34.8 ± 6.5 and 35.2 ± 8.3 min in TYR and PLA, respectively; P = 0.4167) were similar between trials. Thermal sensation (P > 0.05), RPE (P > 0.05), core temperature (P = 0.860), skin temperature (P = 0.822), and heart rate (P = 0.314) did not differ between trials. These data indicate that acute tyrosine administration did not influence self-paced endurance exercise performance in the heat. Plasma tyrosine availability is apparently not a key determinant of fatigue processes under these conditions.

studies.title: Oral tyrosine supplementation improves exercise capacity in the heat.
studies.abstract: Increased brain dopamine availability improves prolonged exercise tolerance in the heat. It is unclear whether supplementing the amino-acid precursor of dopamine increases exercise capacity in the heat. Eight healthy male volunteers [mean age 32 ± 11 (SD) years; body mass 75.3 ± 8.1 kg; peak oxygen uptake ([Formula: see text]) 3.5 ± 0.3 L min(-1)] performed two exercise trials separated by at least 7 days in a randomised, crossover design. Subjects consumed 500 mL of a flavoured sugar-free drink (PLA), or the same drink with 150 mg kg body mass(-1) tyrosine (TYR) in a double-blind manner 1 h before cycling to exhaustion at a constant exercise intensity equivalent to 68 ± 5% [Formula: see text] in 30°C and 60% relative humidity. Pre-exercise plasma tyrosine:large neutral amino acids increased 2.9-fold in TYR (P < 0.01), while there was no change in PLA (P > 0.05). Subjects cycled longer in TYR compared to PLA (80.3 ± 19.7 min vs. 69.2 ± 14.0 min; P < 0.01). Core temperature, mean weighted skin temperature, heart rate, ratings of perceived exertion and thermal sensation were similar in TYR and PLA during exercise and at exhaustion (P > 0.05) despite longer exercise time in TYR. The results show that acute tyrosine supplementation is associated with increased endurance capacity in the heat in moderately trained subjects. The results also suggest for the first time that the availability of tyrosine, a nutritional dopamine precursor, can influence the ability to subjectively tolerate prolonged submaximal constant-load exercise in the heat.

studies.title: Effects of L-tyrosine and carbohydrate ingestion on endurance exercise performance.
studies.abstract: To test the effects of tyrosine ingestion with or without carbohydrate supplementation on endurance performance, nine competitive cyclists cycled at 70% peak oxygen uptake for 90 min under four different feeding conditions followed immediately by a time trial. At 30-min intervals, beginning 60 min before exercise, each subject consumed either 5 ml/kg body wt of water sweetened with aspartame [placebo (Pla)], polydextrose (70 g/l) (CHO), L-tyrosine (25 mg/kg body wt) (Tyr), or polydextrose (70 g/l) and L-tyrosine (25 mg/kg body wt) (CHO+Tyr). The experimental trials were given in random order and were carried out by using a counterbalanced double-blind design. No differences were found between treatments for oxygen uptake, heart rate, or rating of perceived exertion at any time during the 90-min ride. Plasma tyrosine rose significantly from 60 min before exercise to test termination (TT) in Tyr (means +/- SE) (480 +/- 26 micromol) and CHO+Tyr (463 +/- 34 micromol) and was significantly higher in these groups from 30 min before exercise to TT vs. CHO (90 +/- 3 micromol) and Pla (111 +/- 7 micromol) (P < 0.05). Plasma free tryptophan was higher after 90 min of exercise, 15 min into the endurance time trial, and at TT in Tyr (10.1 +/- 0.9, 10.4 +/- 0.8, and 12.0 +/- 0.9 micromol, respectively) and Pla (9.7 +/- 0.5, 10.0 +/- 0.3, and 11.7 +/- 0.5 micromol, respectively) vs. CHO (7.8 +/- 0.5, 8.6 +/- 0.5, and 9.3 +/- 0.6 micromol, respectively) and CHO+Tyr (7.8 +/- 0.5, 8.5 +/- 0.5, 9.4 +/- 0.5 micromol, respectively) (P < 0.05). The plasma tyrosine-to-free tryptophan ratio was significantly higher in Tyr and CHO+Tyr vs. CHO and Pla from 30 min before exercise to TT (P < 0.05). CHO (27.1 +/- 0.9 min) and CHO+Tyr (26.1 +/- 1.1 min) treatments resulted in a reduced time to complete the endurance time trial compared with Pla (34.4 +/- 2.9 min) and Tyr (32.6 +/- 3.0 min) (P < 0.05). These findings demonstrate that tyrosine ingestion did not enhance performance during a cycling time trial after 90 min of steady-state exercise.

studies.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: tactical athlete nutrition.
studies.abstract:
This position stand aims to provide an evidence-based summary of the energy and nutritional demands of tactical athletes to promote optimal health and performance while keeping in mind the unique challenges faced due to work schedules, job demands, and austere environments. After a critical analysis of the literature, the following nutritional guidelines represent the position of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN).

General recommendations

Nutritional considerations should include the provision and timing of adequate calories, macronutrients, and fluid to meet daily needs as well as strategic nutritional supplementation to improve physical, cognitive, and occupational performance outcomes; reduce risk of injury, obesity, and cardiometabolic disease; reduce the potential for a fatal mistake; and promote occupational readiness.

Military recommendations

Energy demands should be met by utilizing the Military Dietary Reference Intakes (MDRIs) established and codified in Army Regulation 40-25. Although research is somewhat limited, military personnel may also benefit from caffeine, creatine monohydrate, essential amino acids, protein, omega-3-fatty acids, beta-alanine, and L-tyrosine supplementation, especially during high-stress conditions.

First responder recommendations

Specific energy needs are unknown and may vary depending on occupation-specific tasks. It is likely the general caloric intake and macronutrient guidelines for recreational athletes or the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges for the general healthy adult population may benefit first responders. Strategies such as implementing wellness policies, setting up supportive food environments, encouraging healthier food systems, and using community resources to offer evidence-based nutrition classes are inexpensive and potentially meaningful ways to improve physical activity and diet habits. The following provides a more detailed overview of the literature and recommendations for these populations.

studies.title: Oral l-tyrosine supplementation augments the vasoconstriction response to whole-body cooling in older adults.
studies.abstract: What is the central question of this study? Ageing is associated with altered sympathetic responses to stress, which are explained in part by reduced noradrenergic function. The impact of supplementation with oral l-tyrosine, the amino acid precursor for catecholamine synthesis, on the effector responses to cold and exercise stress has yet to be examined. What is the main finding and its importance? Oral l-tyrosine ingestion augmented the sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction response to cold exposure in aged skin. This suggests that l-tyrosine supplementation might improve thermoregulatory function in older adults. l-Tyrosine is the primary substrate for noradrenaline biosynthesis within sympathetic axon terminals. In stressful conditions requiring increased catecholamine production, the axonal l-tyrosine concentration may limit the full expression of the sympathetic effector response and this may be particularly evident in older adults. We hypothesize that oral l-tyrosine supplementation will increase the sympathetic response to whole-body cooling and muscle metaboreflex activation. explanation.what_it_is_line: An amino acid your body uses to build neurotransmitters and stress hormones.
explanation.what_it_is: L-tyrosine is one of the 20 standard amino acids — the building blocks your body assembles into proteins. It's particularly notable because your body also uses it as a raw material to manufacture dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine (adrenaline), which are neurotransmitters and hormones involved in alertness, focus, and stress response. You get tyrosine from protein-rich foods (meat, eggs, dairy, nuts) and it's also sold as a dietary supplement in powder or capsule form. It is water-soluble (it loves water more than fat), which is why it absorbs readily when taken by mouth.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Provides raw material for dopamine and stress hormones, potentially sharpening focus under pressure.
explanation.how_it_works: Your brain and adrenal glands use tyrosine as a starting point to manufacture dopamine (a chemical that supports focus, motivation, and working memory) and norepinephrine/epinephrine (stress and alertness hormones). The idea is straightforward: if tyrosine is the rate-limiting ingredient — the one in short supply — then supplementing it might boost production of these compounds, especially under stress or cognitive demand. This mechanism is well-established in biochemistry. Whether supplemental tyrosine actually increases these neurotransmitter levels in humans, and whether that translates to measurable improvements in real-world performance, is what the clinical trials aim to test.
explanation.safety_line: Most trials report mild or no side effects; long-term and drug-interaction data remain limited.
explanation.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved reported tolerability generally good, with no serious adverse events noted in the short durations studied (mostly acute doses or a few weeks). However, trials typically exclude people with certain conditions (kidney disease, thyroid disorder, phenylketonuria), pregnant individuals, and adolescents — so safety in those groups is untested. No large-scale or long-term safety database was provided, and potential interactions with psychiatric medications or thyroid agents were not adequately characterized in the retrieved records.
safety_bullets: Drug interactions: untested with dopamine-active medications (stimulants, antidepressants, dopamine agonists); caution warranted if you take these.
Kidney disease or severe liver disease: excluded from trials; safety unknown, consult provider.
Thyroid disorders: tyrosine is a precursor to thyroid hormone; untested in hyperthyroidism or on thyroid replacement — discuss with clinician.
Pregnancy and adolescence: no safety data in trials; not studied in these groups.
explanation.chem_meaning: L-tyrosine is a small, water-loving amino acid (molecular weight 181), so it dissolves readily in water and is absorbed efficiently by the intestine. Its negative lipophilicity (XLogP −2.3) means it does not easily cross the blood–brain barrier on its own; it relies on an active transporter, which may limit how much reaches the brain even if you consume large doses.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human randomized trials and one observational study (n=1,724 in the dietary cohort) investigated tyrosine's effect on cognitive measures — working memory, mental performance under stress, and everyday cognitive function. A 2020 RCT (n=45) found a baseline-dependent effect on working memory gating; a 2024 RCT (n=28) paired tyrosine with L-theanine and saw cognitive improvements alongside stress markers in response to a virtual reality stressor; a 2017 double-blind crossover trial and a 2026 combined-supplement RCT also reported cognitive benefits. The large observational study (2019) associated higher dietary tyrosine intake with better cognitive performance in younger and older adults.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: All five human trials showed results, but they used different populations, doses, stressors, and cognitive tests, so a pooled conclusion cannot be confirmed yet. Moderate grade reflects promising human evidence tempered by inconsistency and small sample sizes in some trials.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human randomized trials examined tyrosine supplementation and endurance exercise capacity, mostly in heat-stress or mental-fatigue contexts. A 2011 RCT found improved exercise capacity in the heat; a 2026 RCT specifically tested mentally fatigued cyclists and reported endurance benefit; a 2002 study combined tyrosine with carbohydrate and measured endurance exercise performance. However, a 2014 RCT found failure of tyrosine to improve heat-exercise performance, showing the effect is not universal. A 2026 combined-supplement trial and a 2022 sports nutrition position paper also included tyrosine in their analysis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Six human trials provide multiple data points, but sample sizes in the abstracts could not be verified, and mixed results (benefit in some, null in others) suggest the effect may depend on specific conditions (heat, mental fatigue, dose, population). Precision is unconfirmed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human trials examined tyrosine's effect on stress or anxiety markers. A 2024 RCT (n=28) paired L-tyrosine with L-theanine and measured stress markers (likely cortisol or self-reported stress) in response to a virtual reality stressor, finding favorable results. A 2017 RCT tested tyrosine's effect on vasoconstriction response to whole-body cooling in older adults, which is related to sympathetic nervous system activity (part of the stress response).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two human studies, and one has a verified sample of just 28 participants. The evidence is too preliminary to confirm benefit; further testing in larger, dedicated stress-outcome trials is needed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human randomized trials directly tested tyrosine on exercise performance. A 2002 RCT combined L-tyrosine with carbohydrate and measured endurance performance; a 2014 RCT tested tyrosine alone during heat stress and found no improvement; a 2026 RCT combined tyrosine with L-carnosine as an ergogenic strategy and reported benefit. The conflicting 2014 null result suggests context-dependence.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Three trials in humans, but sample sizes are unverified from abstracts and results are mixed. Moderate grade reflects human data with uncertainty about precision and generalizability.

explanation.evidence_base: All evidence is from humans; no animal studies were included in the retrieved records. The evidence comes primarily from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and a few observational or unclassified studies, spanning 2002 to 2026, with most trials acute (single dose or a few weeks). The preponderance of RCT data is reassuring, but sample sizes are often small and not always reported clearly in abstracts. This means we have real human data but lack the large, long-term registries that would cement confidence.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records show trials mostly in young to middle-aged adults (one 2019 cohort included older adults) engaged in exercise or cognitive stress; no trials in children, adolescents, or populations with neuropsychiatric disease were found. Most studies used acute doses or short windows; no long-term supplementation outcomes (weeks to months) were characterized in the sample provided. It remains unclear whether benefit depends on baseline tyrosine status, genetics, or specific stressors. The sample of ~40 abstracts per outcome is a fraction of the published literature — gaps you see here may not reflect the full field.

appraisal.headline: No pooled analyses exist for any outcome; individual trials show inconsistent results and most sample sizes are unverifiable from abstracts, making it impossible to quantify true effect size or confidence.

concerns.detail: Six endurance trials and three exercise performance trials report no extractable n values from abstracts. The cognition outcome reports only 3 of 5 studies with n values (28, 45, 1724). Without sample size verification, standard errors cannot be assessed and small underpowered trials could masquerade as evidence. A single large observational study (n=1724 in cognition) may be inflating confidence in that outcome while contributing confounding via dietary assessment rather than supplementation.

concerns.issue: Conflicting trial outcomes on identical questions
concerns.detail: Endurance shows two 2011/2014 trials with opposite conclusions ('improves' vs. 'failure of' exercise capacity in heat), yet no pooled analysis or head-to-head comparison is documented. Similarly, the 2024 cognition RCT (n=28) combined L-theanine and L-tyrosine, making L-tyrosine's independent contribution unclear. The engine flags 'Inconsistency' for cognition but stops short of resolving which direction the evidence actually points.

concerns.issue: Extreme heterogeneity in cognition evidence base
concerns.detail: One study enrolled 1,724 observational participants (dietary tyrosine intake), while three RCTs ranged from n=28–45. The observational trial uses dietary proxy exposure (not supplementation), confounding interpretation of whether supplemental L-tyrosine replicates the association. No study defines how cognitive outcomes were measured or whether results align across domains (working memory, executive function, etc.).

concerns.issue: Stress/anxiety outcome rests on minimal evidence
concerns.detail: Only two RCTs totaling ~28 verified participants address stress/anxiety (graded 'Emerging'). One 2024 trial again combines L-theanine + L-tyrosine, blocking inference about L-tyrosine alone. The 2017 trial measures vasoconstriction in whole-body cooling—a biomarker, not a clinical stress or anxiety outcome. No trial directly measured anxiety scales or validated stress biomarkers.

concerns.issue: Absence of blinding or allocation concealment detail
concerns.detail: One 2017 trial is labeled 'Double Blind' but the others' methodological quality is not visible in abstracts. High risk of bias from unblinded or inadequately concealed allocation would inflate effect sizes, particularly in small trials (n=28–45 for cognition and stress) where investigators' expectations easily influence measurement.

appraisal.mechanism_check: L-tyrosine is a dopamine precursor, and dopamine supports working memory and arousal under stress—a plausible biological chain. However, the clinical leap is substantial: dietary availability of amino acids does not guarantee cerebral dopamine depletion in the tested populations, nor is it established that oral tyrosine crosses the blood–brain barrier efficiently under the dosing used. The 2020 cognition RCT reports 'baseline-dependent effect on working memory gating but not updating,' suggesting the benefit is narrow and context-dependent, yet endurance and stress outcomes invoke the same precursor logic without verifying whether the same mechanism operates or whether effect sizes replicate.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A well-informed skeptic would note that (1) the two heat-exercise trials contradict each other without resolution; (2) most sample sizes are unverifiable, leaving open the possibility that negative or null trials were excluded from reporting; (3) the largest cognition study is observational (dietary intake proxy, not supplementation) and cannot isolate causality; and (4) stress/anxiety is supported only by a biomarker study and a combination product, neither directly addressing clinical anxiety. The 'Moderate' grades for cognition, endurance, and exercise performance may reflect absence of definitive harm rather than presence of clear benefit.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A pre-registered, adequately powered RCT (n≥100) comparing L-tyrosine vs. placebo in a single, well-defined population (e.g., cognitively normal adults under acute stress or heat-fatigued athletes) with blinded allocation, standardized outcome measures (validated cognitive batteries, exercise time-to-exhaustion), and reported sample size justification would establish whether any single outcome is real. Meta-analysis of existing trials with sensitivity analysis excluding the observational study would clarify whether the inconsistency in endurance and exercise outcomes reflects genuine heterogeneity or small-sample noise.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un aminoácido que tu cuerpo utiliza para construir neurotransmisores y hormonas del estrés.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La L-tirosina es uno de los 20 aminoácidos estándar — los bloques de construcción que tu cuerpo ensambla en proteínas. Es particularmente notable porque tu cuerpo también la utiliza como materia prima para fabricar dopamina, norepinefrina y epinefrina (adrenalina), que son neurotransmisores y hormonas implicados en la alerta, el enfoque y la respuesta al estrés. Obtienes tirosina de alimentos ricos en proteínas (carne, huevos, productos lácteos, nueces) y también se vende como suplemento dietético en forma de polvo o cápsula. Es soluble en agua (ama el agua más que la grasa), por lo que se absorbe fácilmente cuando se ingiere por vía oral.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Proporciona materia prima para la dopamina y las hormonas del estrés, potencialmente agudizando el enfoque bajo presión.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Tu cerebro y glándulas suprarrenales utilizan la tirosina como punto de partida para fabricar dopamina (una sustancia química que respalda el enfoque, la motivación y la memoria de trabajo) y norepinefrina/epinefrina (hormonas de estrés y alerta). La idea es directa: si la tirosina es el ingrediente limitante — el que está en corta disponibilidad — entonces complementarla podría impulsar la producción de estos compuestos, especialmente bajo estrés o demanda cognitiva. Este mecanismo está bien establecido en la bioquímica. Si la tirosina complementaria aumenta realmente los niveles de estos neurotransmisores en humanos, y si eso se traduce en mejoras medibles en el rendimiento del mundo real, es lo que los ensayos clínicos pretenden probar.
explanation_es.safety_line: La mayoría de los ensayos reportan efectos secundarios leves o ninguno; los datos a largo plazo e interacciones farmacológicas siguen siendo limitados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos en humanos recuperados reportaron tolerabilidad generalmente buena, sin eventos adversos graves anotados en las duraciones cortas estudiadas (principalmente dosis agudas o pocas semanas). Sin embargo, los ensayos típicamente excluyen a personas con ciertas condiciones (enfermedad renal, trastorno tiroideo, fenilcetonuria), individuos embarazadas y adolescentes — por lo que la seguridad en esos grupos no ha sido probada. No se proporcionó una base de datos de seguridad grande o a largo plazo, e interacciones potenciales con medicamentos psiquiátricos o agentes tiroideos no fueron adecuadamente caracterizadas en los registros recuperados.
safety_bullets: Interacciones farmacológicas: no probadas con medicamentos activos en dopamina (estimulantes, antidepresivos, agonistas dopaminérgicos); se aconseja precaución si tomas estos.
Enfermedad renal o enfermedad hepática severa: excluidas de los ensayos; seguridad desconocida, consulta con tu proveedor.
Trastornos tiroideos: la tirosina es un precursor de la hormona tiroidea; no probada en hipertiroidismo o en reemplazo tiroideo — discute con tu clínico.
Embarazo y adolescencia: sin datos de seguridad en ensayos; no estudiado en estos grupos.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La L-tirosina es un aminoácido pequeño que ama el agua (peso molecular 181), por lo que se disuelve fácilmente en agua y es absorbida eficientemente por el intestino. Su lipofilia negativa (XLogP −2.3) significa que no cruza fácilmente la barrera hematoencefálica por sí sola; depende de un transportador activo, lo que puede limitar cuánto llega al cerebro incluso si consumes dosis grandes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco ensayos aleatorios en humanos y un estudio observacional (n=1,724 en la cohorte dietética) investigaron el efecto de la tirosina en medidas cognitivas — memoria de trabajo, rendimiento mental bajo estrés y función cognitiva cotidiana. Un ECA de 2020 (n=45) encontró un efecto dependiente de la línea base en el filtrado de memoria de trabajo; un ECA de 2024 (n=28) emparejó tirosina con L-teanina y vio mejoras cognitivas junto con marcadores de estrés en respuesta a un estresor de realidad virtual; un ensayo de doble ciego cruzado de 2017 y un ECA de suplemento combinado de 2026 también reportaron beneficios cognitivos. El gran estudio observacional (2019) asoció una ingesta dietética más alta de tirosina con mejor rendimiento cognitivo en adultos jóvenes y mayores.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Los cinco ensayos en humanos mostraron resultados, pero utilizaron diferentes poblaciones, dosis, estresores y pruebas cognitivas, por lo que una conclusión conjunta no puede confirmarse aún. La calificación Moderada refleja evidencia prometedora en humanos temperada por inconsistencia y tamaños de muestra pequeños en algunos ensayos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seis ensayos aleatorios en humanos examinaron la suplementación con tirosina y la capacidad de ejercicio de resistencia, principalmente en contextos de estrés por calor o fatiga mental. Un ECA de 2011 encontró mejor capacidad de ejercicio en el calor; un ECA de 2026 específicamente probó ciclistas mentalmente fatigados y reportó beneficio de resistencia; un estudio de 2002 combinó tirosina con carbohidrato y midió el rendimiento del ejercicio de resistencia. Sin embargo, un ECA de 2014 encontró fallo de la tirosina para mejorar el rendimiento del ejercicio en calor, mostrando que el efecto no es universal. Un ensayo de suplemento combinado de 2026 y un documento de posición de nutrición deportiva de 2022 también incluyen tirosina en su análisis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Seis ensayos en humanos proporcionan múltiples puntos de datos, pero los tamaños de muestra en los resúmenes no pudieron verificarse, y resultados mixtos (beneficio en algunos, nulo en otros) sugieren que el efecto puede depender de condiciones específicas (calor, fatiga mental, dosis, población). La precisión no está confirmada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dos ensayos en humanos examinaron el efecto de la tirosina en marcadores de estrés o ansiedad. Un ECA de 2024 (n=28) emparejó L-tirosina con L-teanina y midió marcadores de estrés (probablemente cortisol o estrés autoreportado) en respuesta a un estresor de realidad virtual, encontrando resultados favorables. Un ECA de 2017 probó el efecto de la tirosina en la respuesta de vasoconstricción al enfriamiento de todo el cuerpo en adultos mayores, lo cual está relacionado con la actividad del sistema nervioso simpático (parte de la respuesta al estrés).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo dos estudios en humanos, y uno tiene una muestra verificada de apenas 28 participantes. La evidencia es demasiado preliminar para confirmar beneficio; se necesita más pruebas en ensayos más grandes y dedicados a resultados de estrés.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres ensayos aleatorios en humanos probaron directamente la tirosina en el rendimiento del ejercicio. Un ECA de 2002 combinó L-tirosina con carbohidrato y midió rendimiento de resistencia; un ECA de 2014 probó tirosina sola durante estrés por calor y no encontró mejora; un ECA de 2026 combinó tirosina con L-carnosina como estrategia ergogénica y reportó beneficio. El resultado nulo conflictivo de 2014 sugiere dependencia del contexto.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Tres ensayos en humanos, pero los tamaños de muestra no están verificados desde los resúmenes y los resultados son mixtos. La calificación Moderada refleja datos en humanos con incertidumbre sobre precisión y generalizabilidad.

explanation_es.evidence_base: Toda la evidencia es de humanos; no se incluyeron estudios en animales en los registros recuperados. La evidencia proviene principalmente de ensayos controlados aleatorios (ECA) y algunos estudios observacionales o no clasificados, abarcando 2002 a 2026, con la mayoría de ensayos agudos (dosis única o pocas semanas). La preponderancia de datos de ECA es tranquilizadora, pero los tamaños de muestra suelen ser pequeños y no siempre se reportan claramente en los resúmenes. Esto significa que tenemos datos reales en humanos pero carecemos de los registros grandes y a largo plazo que cimentarían la confianza.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados muestran ensayos principalmente en adultos jóvenes a mediana edad (una cohorte de 2019 incluyó adultos mayores) comprometidos en ejercicio o estrés cognitivo; no se encontraron ensayos en niños, adolescentes o poblaciones con enfermedad neuropsiquiátrica. La mayoría de los estudios utilizaron dosis agudas o ventanas cortas; no se caracterizaron resultados de suplementación a largo plazo (semanas a meses) en la muestra proporcionada. Sigue siendo incierto si el beneficio depende del estado basal de tirosina, genética o estresores específicos. La muestra de ~40 resúmenes por resultado es una fracción de la literatura publicada — las brechas que ves aquí pueden no reflejar el campo completo.

appraisal_es.headline: No existen análisis agrupados para ningún resultado; los ensayos individuales muestran resultados inconsistentes y la mayoría de los tamaños de muestra no son verificables a partir de resúmenes, lo que hace imposible cuantificar el tamaño del efecto verdadero o la confianza.

concerns.issue: Opacidad sistemática de los tamaños de muestra
concerns.detail: Seis ensayos de resistencia y tres ensayos de rendimiento del ejercicio no reportan valores de n extraíbles de los resúmenes. El resultado de cognición reporta solo 3 de 5 estudios con valores de n (28, 45, 1724). Sin verificación del tamaño de muestra, los errores estándar no pueden evaluarse y los ensayos pequeños y sin poder estadístico podrían pasar por evidencia. Un único estudio observacional grande (n=1724 en cognición) podría estar inflando la confianza en ese resultado mientras contribuye con confusión a través de la evaluación dietética en lugar de la suplementación.

concerns.issue: Resultados de ensayos conflictivos en preguntas idénticas
concerns.detail: La resistencia muestra dos ensayos de 2011/2014 con conclusiones opuestas ('mejora' vs. 'fracaso de' la capacidad de ejercicio en calor), pero no se documenta análisis agrupado ni comparación directa. De manera similar, el ECA de cognición de 2024 (n=28) combinó L-teanina y L-tirosina, lo que hace que la contribución independiente de L-tirosina sea poco clara. El motor marca 'Inconsistencia' para cognición pero no llega a resolver en qué dirección apunta realmente la evidencia.

concerns.issue: Heterogeneidad extrema en la base de evidencia de cognición
concerns.detail: Un estudio incluyó 1.724 participantes observacionales (ingesta dietética de tirosina), mientras que tres ECA variaron de n=28–45. El ensayo observacional utiliza exposición dietética como proxy (no suplementación), confundiendo la interpretación de si la L-tirosina suplementaria replica la asociación. Ningún estudio define cómo se midieron los resultados cognitivos o si los resultados se alinean entre dominios (memoria de trabajo, función ejecutiva, etc.).

concerns.issue: El resultado de estrés/ansiedad descansa sobre evidencia mínima
concerns.detail: Solo dos ECA totalizando ~28 participantes verificados abordan estrés/ansiedad (clasificados como 'Emergente'). Un ensayo de 2024 nuevamente combina L-teanina + L-tirosina, bloqueando la inferencia sobre L-tirosina sola. El ensayo de 2017 mide vasoconstricción en enfriamiento de cuerpo completo—un biomarcador, no un resultado clínico de estrés o ansiedad. Ningún ensayo midió directamente escalas de ansiedad o biomarcadores de estrés validados.

concerns.issue: Ausencia de detalles de enmascaramiento u ocultamiento de asignación
concerns.detail: Un ensayo de 2017 está etiquetado como 'Doble Ciego' pero la calidad metodológica de los otros no es visible en los resúmenes. El alto riesgo de sesgo por asignación no enmascarada o inadecuadamente ocultada inflaría los tamaños del efecto, particularmente en ensayos pequeños (n=28–45 para cognición y estrés) donde las expectativas de los investigadores influyen fácilmente en la medición.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: La L-tirosina es un precursor de dopamina, y la dopamina respalda la memoria de trabajo y la excitación bajo estrés—una cadena biológica plausible. Sin embargo, el salto clínico es sustancial: la disponibilidad dietética de aminoácidos no garantiza depleción de dopamina cerebral en las poblaciones probadas, ni está establecido que la tirosina oral cruce eficientemente la barrera hematoencefálica bajo las dosis utilizadas. El ECA de cognición de 2020 reporta 'efecto dependiente de la línea base en la compuerta de la memoria de trabajo pero no en actualización', sugiriendo que el beneficio es estrecho y dependiente del contexto, pero los resultados de resistencia y estrés invocan la misma lógica de precursor sin verificar si el mismo mecanismo opera o si los tamaños del efecto se replican.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico bien informado notaría que (1) los dos ensayos de ejercicio en calor se contradicen entre sí sin resolución; (2) la mayoría de los tamaños de muestra no son verificables, dejando abierta la posibilidad de que ensayos negativos o nulos fueran excluidos del reporte; (3) el estudio más grande de cognición es observacional (proxy de ingesta dietética, no suplementación) y no puede aislar causalidad; y (4) estrés/ansiedad es apoyado solo por un estudio de biomarcadores y un producto combinado, ninguno abordando directamente la ansiedad clínica. Las clasificaciones 'Moderada' para cognición, resistencia y rendimiento del ejercicio pueden reflejar ausencia de daño definitivo en lugar de presencia de beneficio claro.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ECA preregistrado, adecuadamente potenciado (n≥100) comparando L-tirosina vs. placebo en una única población bien definida (p. ej., adultos cognitivamente normales bajo estrés agudo o atletas fatigados por calor) con asignación enmascarada, medidas de resultado estandarizadas (baterías cognitivas validadas, tiempo al agotamiento del ejercicio) e justificación del tamaño de muestra reportada establecería si algún resultado único es real. Metanálisis de ensayos existentes con análisis de sensibilidad excluyendo el estudio observacional aclararía si la inconsistencia en resultados de resistencia y ejercicio refleja heterogeneidad genuina o ruido de muestra pequeña.
